CHAPTER 1
WHAT THE HECK IS NETWORK MARKETING?
WHAT IS NETWORK MARKETING?
Network marketing is a way of selling products or services
through people and their personal networks.
Instead of a company relying only on traditional advertising, it
can allow individuals to introduce its products to other people.
When someone makes a qualifying purchase through that
referral, the person who made the referral may receive a
commission or reward based on the company's terms.
In simple terms:
You discover a product.
You use or understand the product.
You tell other people about it.
Someone you referred becomes a customer.
You may receive a reward for that referral.
That's network marketing in its simplest form.
MEET ZOE
Zoe was an ordinary young woman trying to figure life out.
Like many people, she had bills to pay, things she wanted to
buy, and plans for her future. She had a phone, an internet
connection, and plenty of people in her WhatsApp contacts,
but she had never really thought of these things as tools she
could use to create an income opportunity.
One day, Zoe came across something she had heard about
before: network marketing.
At first, she was confused.
"What exactly is network marketing?"
She had heard people talk about referrals, commissions and
sharing products, but she had never taken the time to
understand how it actually worked.
So she decided to learn.
As Zoe discovered, network marketing is not simply about
sending a link to everyone in your contacts. It is about
understanding what you are offering, finding people who may
genuinely be interested, explaining it clearly and giving them
the freedom to decide.
And that is where Zoe's journey begins.
CHAPTER 2
THE DIGITAL ASSET
WHAT IS A DIGITAL ASSET?
When most people hear the word "asset," they think about
land, a car, a house or something physical that has value.
But not every asset has to be something you can touch.
A digital asset is something valuable that exists in digital
form. It can be an eBook, online course, software, design,
video, website, template or other digital product that people
can access through the internet.
This is where things get interesting.
A digital product can be created once and shared with many
people without needing a physical shop, warehouse or
delivery truck.
For example, imagine you write a useful eBook about
budgeting. Once the book is ready, someone in Nairobi can
read it today, while another person in Mombasa can access
the same book tomorrow.
The product is digital, but the value is real.
That is the idea behind BookVerse.
BookVerse is built around digital books and the opportunities
that can come from sharing useful digital products with other
people.
Instead of thinking only about what you can sell physically,
you can also learn how to work with products that can be
delivered through a phone.
YOUR PHONE IS MORE THAN A PHONE
Think about how much time people spend on their phones
every day.
We use them to chat, watch videos, check social media, send
money, shop, learn and look for opportunities.
The same phone can also become a tool for a side hustle.
You don't need to become a full-time salesperson. You don't
need to walk around knocking on people's doors.
You can learn about a digital product, understand who it may
be useful to, and introduce it to people through platforms you
already use, such as WhatsApp.
That's the part Zoe began to understand.
She didn't need to change her entire life.
She simply needed to learn how to use the tools already in her
hands.
THE VALUE IS IN THE PRODUCT
One important lesson Zoe learned was that referrals work best
when there is something worth sharing.
People are not interested in a link simply because it is a link.
They want to know:
"What am I getting?"
"Is it useful to me?"
"Why should I care?"
That's why understanding the product comes first.
Before Zoe started sharing BookVerse, she took time to
understand what it offered, who it was designed for and how
the referral system worked.
That made her conversations much easier.
She wasn't just sending random messages.
She was sharing something she understood.
A DIGITAL ASSET CAN TRAVEL
One of the biggest advantages of digital products is
accessibility.
A physical product may need packaging, transport and
storage.
A digital product can be accessed through a phone or
computer from almost anywhere with an internet connection.
This doesn't mean every digital product will succeed.
It simply means the way we create, distribute and discover
products has changed.
And for someone looking for a side hustle, that creates an
interesting opportunity to explore.
ZOE'S FIRST LESSON
Zoe realized that the real opportunity wasn't simply having a
phone.
Millions of people have phones.
The difference comes from learning how to use that phone
productively.
For Zoe, BookVerse became a starting point.
She would learn about digital products, learn how referrals
work, share what she understood and build from there — all
while continuing with her normal life.
That is the mindset behind this book.
You are not looking for a magic button.
You are learning a skill.
CHAPTER 3
UNDERSTANDING THE REFERRAL MODEL
Now Zoe understood what a digital product was. The next
question was simple:
"How does the referral part actually work?"
THE BASIC IDEA
A referral is simply recommending something to another
person using your unique referral link or code.
Think about everyday life.
Your friend asks you:
"Which phone shop do you trust?"
You recommend one.
Your cousin asks:
"Which restaurant do you like?"
You give them a name.
Your friend asks:
"Where did you get that course?"
You send them the link.
These are all forms of referrals.
The difference with a referral business is that the company can
track who introduced a new customer. If that person
completes the required action, the person who made the
referral may receive a commission or reward according to the
current terms.
HOW BOOKVERSE WORKS
BookVerse keeps the process simple.
You become an active BookVerse member.
You receive your personal referral link.
You share that link with people who may be interested.
When someone joins through your link and completes the
required activation, the system records the referral.
If the referral qualifies under BookVerse's current terms, you
receive the applicable referral reward.
That's it.
There is no need to make the process complicated.
YOUR LINK MATTERS
Your referral link is like your digital introduction.
When you send someone your link, BookVerse can identify
that the person came through you.
This is why you should always use your own referral link when
introducing someone to the platform.
Don't copy another person's link.
Don't create fake accounts to make your numbers look bigger.
And don't pressure people into joining just because you want
a referral.
PEOPLE COME FIRST
Zoe learned something important.
A referral is not just a number on a dashboard.
There is a real person on the other side of every link.
That person should understand what they are joining before
they make a decision.
If someone asks questions, Zoe answers honestly.
If she doesn't know the answer, she finds out.
If someone isn't interested, she moves on.
This approach helped her feel more comfortable sharing
BookVerse because she wasn't trying to convince everyone.
She was simply introducing people to something they could
choose to explore.
DON'T BUILD YOUR HUSTLE AROUND SPAM
There is a big difference between sharing and spamming.
Sharing means telling someone about something that may
genuinely interest them.
Spamming means sending the same message repeatedly to
people who have shown no interest.
Nobody likes receiving ten messages saying:
"JOIN NOW!!!"
"LAST CHANCE!!!"
"YOU ARE MISSING OUT!!!"
Zoe decided she didn't want to build her side hustle that way.
She would rather have a few genuine conversations than
annoy hundreds of people.
THE SIMPLE FORMULA
Remember this:
UNDERSTAND → SHARE → EXPLAIN → REFER
Understand what you're offering.
Share it with the right people.
Explain how it works.
Let interested people use your referral link.
That's the referral model.
Simple enough to understand.
But like any side hustle, the results depend on your
consistency, communication and the people you reach.
For Zoe, this was only the beginning.
CHAPTER 4
THE ZOE PLAYBOOK
Zoe now understood what BookVerse was about.
She understood digital products. She understood referrals. But
knowing how something works is different from knowing how
to actually do it.
Her next question was:
"How do I get people interested without becoming that person
who sends everyone random links?"
START WITH PEOPLE YOU KNOW
Zoe started with the people already around her.
She looked through her WhatsApp contacts and thought
about who might actually be interested in digital products,
learning new skills or exploring a side hustle.
She didn't message everyone at once.
She picked a few people and started conversations.
This is an important lesson when starting any side hustle: you
don't need hundreds of people on day one.
Start with the network you already have.
DON'T LEAD WITH THE LINK
One mistake beginners make is sending a referral link before
explaining anything.
Imagine receiving a message from someone that simply says:
"Join this. Here's my link."
You would probably ask:
"What is it?"
Zoe learned to do things differently.
She would start with a simple conversation.
She might say:
"Hey, have you ever looked into digital products as a side
hustle?"
If the person showed interest, she would explain BookVerse
and what it offers.
Only after the person understood the idea would she share her
referral link.
EXPLAIN, DON'T PRESSURE
Zoe also learned that she didn't have to convince everyone.
Some people would be interested.
Some would have questions.
Some would say no.
And that's completely normal.
Her job was simply to explain the opportunity clearly and let
the other person decide.
A good referral conversation should never feel like someone is
being forced into something.
Trust is more valuable than one quick referral.
USE WHATSAPP PROPERLY
For Zoe, WhatsApp became one of her main tools.
She could use her status to introduce BookVerse.
She could have one-to-one conversations with interested
people.
She could answer questions.
She could follow up with someone who had already shown
interest.
The important thing was to use WhatsApp as a
communication tool, not a spam machine.
THE THREE-STEP METHOD
Zoe eventually developed a simple routine:
1. CREATE CURIOSITY
Post something that makes people curious about what you're
doing.
2. START A CONVERSATION
When someone asks about it, explain what BookVerse is and
what they can expect.
3. SHARE YOUR LINK
If they're genuinely interested, send them your personal
referral link so they can take the next step.
KEEP IT NATURAL
You don't need to sound like a professional salesperson.
Talk normally.
Use the language you would actually use when speaking to a
friend.
Instead of:
"Dear esteemed prospect, I would like to introduce you to an

Just say:
"Hey, I've been trying something new with digital products.
Want me to show you how it works?"
ZOE'S RULE
Zoe made one rule for herself:
"Never promise what I cannot guarantee."
She would never tell someone they were guaranteed to make
money.
She would never pretend everyone would succeed.
She would simply explain the product, explain how the referral
system works and let people make their own decisions.
That made her more comfortable sharing.
And more importantly, it made people more comfortable
listening.
THE REAL PLAYBOOK
Understand the product.
Talk to the right people.
Create genuine conversations.
Explain clearly.
Share your link when someone is interested.
Follow up without pressure.
Then keep going.
That's how Zoe decided to approach her side hustle.

START WITH YOUR OWN CIRCLE

Friends.
Former classmates.
Workmates.
Family members.
People she regularly interacted with on WhatsApp.
These were people who already knew her, which made

MAKE A SIMPLE LIST
Zoe opened her phone and created a small list.
She wrote down the names of people who might be interested
in digital products, reading, learning new things or exploring a
side hustle.
She didn't assume that everyone on the list would join.
The purpose was simply to know who she could approach.
You can do the same.
Write down your first 10 people.
Don't overthink it.

QUALITY OVER QUANTITY
Zoe quickly discovered that sending messages to 100 people
wasn't necessarily better than having five genuine
conversations.
One person might ask questions.
Another might not be interested.
Someone else might join immediately.
Everyone is different.
The important thing is to focus on having real conversations

DON'T CHASE PEOPLE
If someone says they're not interested, respect their answer.
If someone says they'll think about it, give them time.
If someone asks questions, answer them honestly.
A person who joins because they understand and genuinely
want to participate is much better than someone who joins
because they were pressured.
Zoe wanted to build a network based on trust, not pressure.
YOUR NETWORK CAN GROW NATURALLY
Your first few referrals don't have to be the end.
Someone you introduce to BookVerse may later introduce
another person.
That person may introduce someone else.
This is how networks can grow.
But don't become obsessed with making your network bigger

Focus on helping the people you bring in understand what
they're doing.
Teach them how to use their referral link.
Show them how to communicate properly.
Share the lessons you've learned.
When people understand the process, they can decide for
themselves whether they want to continue.
ZOE'S FIRST TARGET
Zoe decided to keep things simple.
Instead of saying:
"I need to get 100 people."
She told herself:
"I'll start with three."
Three people she could genuinely talk to.
Three people she could explain BookVerse to.
Three people she could answer questions for.
Once she finished, she could repeat the process.
YOUR TURN
Take out your phone or a piece of paper.
Write down three people you could introduce to BookVerse.
Don't choose people because you think you can pressure them
into joining.
Choose people who might genuinely find the product or the
idea useful.
Then start a conversation.
That's how Zoe built her first network — one conversation at a
time.
CHAPTER 7
HOW TO FOLLOW UP
Zoe soon discovered that getting someone interested was only
the beginning.
Sometimes a person would ask for the link and then
disappear.
Sometimes they would say:
"Let me think about it."
Sometimes they would read the message and never reply.
At first, Zoe thought she had done something wrong.
Then she realized something important:
Not everyone is ready to make a decision immediately.
FOLLOW-UP IS NOT CHASING
Following up simply means checking back with someone who
has already shown interest.
It doesn't mean sending five messages in one day.
It doesn't mean begging someone to join.
And it definitely doesn't mean making someone feel guilty for
saying no.
Zoe learned to keep her follow-ups short and respectful.
A SIMPLE FOLLOW-UP
For someone who asked for information, Zoe could say:
"Hey, just checking in. Did you get a chance to look at the
BookVerse information I sent you?"
IF THEY HAVE QUESTIONS
Sometimes people don't need another sales message.
They simply need an answer.
If someone says:
"I'm not sure how the referral part works."
Zoe explains it.
If they ask:
"What do I get when I join?"
She explains what BookVerse currently offers.
If she doesn't know the answer, she doesn't make one up.
She finds the correct information first.
IF THEY SAY "I'LL THINK ABOUT IT"
Zoe doesn't argue.
She simply says:
"No problem. Take your time. If you have any questions later,
just let me know."
IF THEY SAY NO
This is one of the most important lessons.
A "no" is a no.
Zoe doesn't keep messaging the person every few days hoping
they'll change their mind.
She respects the decision and moves on.
There are plenty of other people she can talk to.
WHEN SHOULD YOU FOLLOW UP?
A simple approach is enough.
First message:
Introduce BookVerse and explain the idea.
Second message:
Follow up after they've had time to look at the information.
Third message:
Answer any questions they have.
After that, let the person decide.
You don't need to turn every conversation into a long sales
pitch.
KEEP TRACK OF YOUR CONVERSATIONS
Zoe started keeping a simple list on her phone.
She would note:
• Who she had contacted
• Who was interested
• Who had received the link
• Who had questions
• Who had already decided not to join
This helped her stay organized.
She didn't have to rely on memory or send the same message
twice.
THE GOAL IS TRUST
Zoe realized that good follow-up isn't about being persistent
at all costs.
It's about being available.
When people know you will answer their questions honestly
and respect their decisions, they are more comfortable dealing
with you.
That's the kind of network Zoe wanted to build.
Not one based on pressure.
One based on trust.
ZOE'S RULE
Her rule became simple:
FOLLOW UP, DON'T CHASE.
Send the message.
Give them time.
Answer questions.
Respect their decision.
Then continue talking to other people.
That's how a side hustle stays enjoyable instead of becoming a
source of stress.
CHAPTER 8
COMMON MISTAKES TO AVOID
By this point, Zoe had learned that building a side hustle was
not only about knowing what to do.
It was also about knowing what NOT to do.
When people are excited about a new opportunity, it is easy
to make mistakes. Zoe made a few herself, but each one
taught her something useful.
MISTAKE 1 — SPAMMING EVERYONE
Zoe once thought the more people she messaged, the better.
She copied the same message and sent it to almost everyone
in her contacts.
The result?
People ignored her.
Some even asked her to stop sending them messages.
She learned that reaching the right people is more important
than reaching everyone.
Talk to people who may actually be interested.
MISTAKE 2 — PROMISING EASY MONEY
This was one mistake Zoe decided never to make again.
She had seen people online making big claims about how
much money someone could make.
But nobody can honestly guarantee another person's results.
Your results depend on many things, including your effort,
communication, consistency and the people you reach.
So instead of saying:
"You will definitely make money."
Zoe would say:
"This is how the referral system works. You can decide if it's
something you want to try."
MISTAKE 3 — NOT UNDERSTANDING THE PRODUCT
Imagine recommending something when you can't answer
basic questions about it.
It makes people lose confidence quickly.
Zoe made sure she understood BookVerse before talking
about it.
She knew what the platform offered, how the referral system
worked and where people could get more information.
The better you understand what you're sharing, the easier it
becomes to explain.
MISTAKE 4 — PRESSURING FRIENDS
Zoe learned that friendship and business should still have
boundaries.
If a friend wasn't interested, she respected that.
She didn't use friendship to pressure someone into joining.
A referral should be an invitation, not an obligation.
MISTAKE 5 — GIVING UP TOO EARLY
Another mistake Zoe almost made was expecting immediate
results.
She would send a few messages and wonder why nothing
happened.
But a side hustle takes time to learn.
Some days she would have good conversations.
Other days, nobody would respond.
That didn't mean the idea was useless.
It simply meant she needed to keep learning and improve how
she communicated.
MISTAKE 6 — SPENDING ALL DAY ON IT
Zoe remembered why she started.
This was a side hustle.
She still had other responsibilities.
She didn't need to spend the entire day checking her phone or
chasing referrals.
She created time for BookVerse around her normal routine.
A side hustle should fit into your life, not completely take over
your life.
MISTAKE 7 — COMPARING YOURSELF TO OTHERS
Zoe noticed that some people seemed to grow much faster
than she did.
Instead of getting discouraged, she stopped comparing her
journey with theirs.
Everyone has a different network, schedule, experience and
starting point.
She focused on improving her own numbers and skills.
THE LESSON
Zoe eventually understood that success wasn't about being
the loudest person online.
It was about being consistent, honest and willing to learn.
Avoid spam.
Avoid unrealistic promises.
Understand what you're sharing.
Respect people's decisions.
Manage your time.
Keep learning.
These simple habits can make a big difference when you're
building a side hustle.
